concepts.bodyMd:
After Brahmananda Reddy's resignation, the Telangana leadership question resurfaced, with Chowkar Rao, Vengala Rao, and P.V. Narasimha Rao as contenders. When P.V. was chosen as leader, the Brahmananda Reddy faction cooperated with the ruling faction, and his government took the oath on **21 September 1971**.

Sanjeevaiah and Raghuramaiah, both national-level leaders, ensured Brahmananda Reddy's supporters did not get ministerial berths, leaving that faction dissatisfied. Previously sidelined sections gained prominence in the ministry for the first time.

General elections to the Andhra Pradesh Assembly were held in **February 1972**. Backward classes, minorities, Harijans, and women together were allotted about **60% of the seats**, and for the first time forward castes and wealthier sections saw their ministry representation reduced. **B.V. Subba Reddy** became Deputy Chief Minister.

Two developments stood out from this period:

*   Generous land grants made by earlier ministerial groups came under scrutiny.
*   Two Panchayati Raj bodies, seen as fronts for landholders, faced Congress attempts at abolition.

P.V. knew that although Indira Gandhi's support — not forward-caste strength — had made him Chief Minister, retaining the post needed the cooperation of the Kamma, Reddy, and Velama castes, support he could not always count on. He therefore tactically drew Harijans, tribal groups, backward classes, and minorities toward himself.

This weakened the landholding classes' grip and allowed the landless among these castes to drift away — a drift that contributed to the strengthening of the separate Andhra movement.

### Land Reforms

The Andhra Pradesh government issued an ordinance banning acquisition of agricultural land beyond a ceiling:

*   **18 acres** on wet lands
*   **34 acres** on dry lands

This struck a hard blow at landholders, since political decentralisation was not possible without economic decentralisation. The ordinance issued on **3 May 1972** tried to block a coming land bill, but there was no courage to act on it openly.

The government announced in **December 1972** that it would pass the bill and implement it. Since the Panchayati Raj system could not cooperate with these reforms, attempts were made to change its structure.

The Land Reforms Bill was finalised in **September 1972**. A Select Committee report followed, and both houses of the legislature passed the bill by large majorities. Just as the ground seemed set for enforcement, the Supreme Court's Mulki Rules verdict intervened (below).

### The Mulki Rules Verdict and Its Fallout

Three Andhra Pradesh High Court judges had, on **12 December 1970**, ruled the Mulki Rules invalid; six judges reversed this ruling on **4 February 1972**. The P.V. government appealed to the Supreme Court, hoping the High Court's decision would be upheld in the state government's favour.

**Cause:** the Supreme Court, on **3 October 1972**, upheld the validity of the Mulki Rules → **Effect:** this created major problems for the state government. Chief Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao called it the final word on Telangana people's rights, but it angered people in the Andhra region.

Landholders used the verdict as a fresh pretext to avoid enforcing the land ceiling law. Agitators mobilised to resist it in several ways:

*   Some convened meetings of landholders opposing the law.
*   Others held meetings in support of landless labourers.
*   Some declared minors in the family as adults, so land could be split across more individual shareholders.
*   Some hastily married off minor daughters, for the same purpose of creating more individual landholders.
*   Some declared their lands to be under mortgage to evade the ceiling.

These same groups both resisted the land law and joined the separate-Andhra agitation. The Chief Minister, Andhra ministers, and Telangana ministers began negotiating separately with each other as the Andhra region reached breaking point.

Telangana and Andhra ministers, honouring earlier promises, together persuaded Indira Gandhi to announce the **Panchasutra (Five-Point) scheme**.

### The Panchasutra (Five-Point) Scheme

1.  Mulki-Rule reservations would apply to non-gazetted employees, Naib Tehsildars, Assistant Surgeons, and Junior Engineers in Telangana — in the Secretariat, one in three vacancies at departmental-head offices and two in three vacancies at district-level offices would fall under this reservation.
2.  These protections would remain until **1980** in Telangana, and until **1987** in the twin cities.
3.  Regularisation could extend to promotion-related services up to the first or second gazetted grade.
4.  Technical education opportunities for Telangana people would expand, with no domicile-based restriction on new admissions.
5.  A joint police cadre would be created for the twin cities.

This scheme, aimed specifically at Junior Engineers and Assistant Civil Servants, was only a compromise and not a permanent solution. The people did not accept it, and demand for a separate Andhra State grew louder.

### Six-Point Formula and P.V.'s Exit

As demand for a separate Andhra State continued, several Andhra ministers resigned. On **11 January 1973**, Madduri Subbareddy, Anam Venkatareddy, G. Someshwar, C. Das, Vadde Nageshwara Rao, R. Rajagopala Reddy, and N. Amaranatha Reddy were appointed as new ministers.

On the same day, the state Congress working committee was dissolved and an emergency committee formed, signalling President's Rule. On the Prime Minister's directive, **P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned on 17 January 1973**.

**President's Rule** began on **18 January 1973**, with H.C. Sarin and V.K. Rao as Governor's advisors. From 18 January to 13 December 1973 — **320 days** — the state remained under President's Rule, with the Assembly suspended.

Andhra-Telangana leaders formulated the **Six-Point Formula** to preserve state unity while addressing all regions' needs.

### The Six-Point Formula

Under this formula, Telangana no longer needed a regional council or the Mulki Rules; abolishing either would not harm Telangana's people's rights.

*   For direct recruitment of non-gazetted employees, Tehsildars, Junior Engineers, and Assistant Surgeons, local candidates would get priority, with the first two promotions going by regional seniority.
*   Three regional zones would be created, each with a regional development board.
*   A Central University would be established with central funding to expand education in the state.
*   A Tribunal would examine employees' grievances, with its decisions treated as final.
*   The capital city would grow in a planned manner, giving twin-city residents priority for employment.
*   Backward regions would receive generous central financial assistance, prioritising mid-range irrigation and rural electrification.
*   All backward regions would be brought to the general development level within a fixed period, with rapid agricultural development targeted for Telangana.

Development-board areas in Telangana, Rayalaseema, and Andhra received ₹100 crore in central funding, including ₹10 crore for Hyderabad city. These funds were distributed at a **5:3:2 ratio** among 162 backward taluks across the three regions, with the scheme due for completion by **31 March 1979**. Regional council chairmen would hold ministerial rank.

P.V. played the main role in shaping this scheme, which received full approval. Andhra Congress leaders, tired of the agitation, sought power, and Congress legislators grew impatient with President's Rule; a special session unanimously approved the Six-Point Formula in the legislature.

Since Andhra leaders insisted P.V.'s leadership must go, he did not get the chance to prove his majority. The **1973 Six-Point Formula** brought a political settlement, and things proceeded peacefully for a while — though the separate Telangana movement kept simmering underground.

**Jalagam Vengala Rao** was elected Chief Minister on **10 December 1973**, succeeding P.V. Narasimha Rao. Compared to most Chief Ministers, there was little doubt about his suitability.

In the favourable circumstances of the Emergency, he continued in power without facing party dissent, working hard both to strengthen himself and for state development. Political rivalry eased partly because Brahmananda Reddy was given a union ministerial berth, Chenna Reddy was appointed Governor of Uttar Pradesh, and P.V. left the state as AICC General Secretary. **B.V. Subba Reddy** became Deputy Chief Minister.

Vengala Rao understood well the trouble the land-ceiling law had created and its effect on the separate Andhra movement, so he thought through new schemes carefully before introducing them. Like Narasimha Rao, he lacked a distinct group of his own and needed the Kamma, Reddy, and Velama castes' cooperation to continue.

He was not a natural reformer by temperament, nor capable of pushing through radical change. Some considered him radical only because his views aligned with weaker sections' sentiments, but he was not fundamentally radical.

Although he did not obstruct caste and political violence, and did not actively encourage it, rumours of ministry expansion spread. Quarrels broke out among competing-faction ministers in each district, and in districts with two ministers, factional rivalries became uncontrollable, with mutual accusations over whatever went wrong.

Vengala Rao organised the first-ever **World Telugu Conference in 1975**. Under Sanjay Gandhi's push, police and official excesses during the Emergency reflected the distortions of his administration, and coercive sterilisation drives also caused him trouble.

The **Nagarjuna Sagar collapse on 19 November 1977**, with no advance-warning systems in place, killed about **10,000 people**.

### Janata Party

In **March 1977**, the old Congress, Jana Sangh, Bharatiya Lok Dal, and Socialist Party united to form the **Janata Party**, which had little strength in the state at the time. All those opposed to Narasimha Rao's and Vengala Rao's actions joined it.

Janata's strength came from three sources:

*   **Urban students**, who saw Congress as authoritarian and Janata as democracy's protector.
*   **Those hurt by land-ceiling enforcement and the loss of bonded-labour arrangements** — mainly wealthy agricultural Reddy families.
*   Political and psychological factors that also drove support toward Janata.

After Andhra Pradesh's formation, the Reddy community had led politically, but this gradually diminished as Kamma, Kapu, and Velama dominance grew. Andhra-Rayalaseema Reddys got reduced representation under Vengala Rao, and his government's abolition of Panchayati Raj posts — disproportionately Reddy-held — hurt the community further.

For these reasons, traditionally Congress-supporting landholding interests began strengthening the Janata Party, mainly through disaffected former Congress workers tired of Congress rule and looking for a new party.

### Congress's Severe Defeat

In the **1977 Lok Sabha elections**, Congress won only **153 seats**, while the Janata Party and its allied Democratic Congress won **298 seats**. The Janata wave swept the northern states but did not fully materialise in the south.

Still, Janata did not fail entirely in Andhra Pradesh — its candidates placed second in nearly every constituency it lost, most receiving over a lakh votes. **Indira Gandhi, who lost the election, resigned as Prime Minister on 23 March 1977**.

This brought a non-Congress (Janata) coalition to power at the Centre for the first time, establishing a lasting trend in India's political culture. Anti-establishment sentiment strengthened nationally, and regional parties in various states gained power by defeating Congress. This 1977 political legacy continues, and the roots of many current ruling parties, state and central, trace back to the Janata Party.

**Morarji Desai** took the oath as India's fourth Prime Minister on **24 March 1977**, but his stubbornness, outdated attitudes, and mistrust of colleagues quickly fractured Janata's unity. He resigned on **15 July 1979**.

**Charan Singh** then became Prime Minister with Indira Gandhi's support; when she withdrew that support, his government lasted only **24 days**. President Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy dissolved the Lok Sabha on **27 August 1979** and ordered mid-term elections — there was no precedent, as in the states, for President's Rule at the Centre.

### Kasu Brahmananda Reddy as Congress President

**Kasu Brahmananda Reddy** contested for the Congress presidency for the first time in 28 years, on **7 May 1977**, receiving **317 votes** against rival Siddhartha Shankar Ray's **160**. Indira Gandhi, in political exile, set about splitting Congress for the second time — eight Congress presidents had already changed in the preceding eight years.

Kasu said Indira Gandhi began campaigning for reinstatement within just three months of becoming Congress president, in order to keep loyalists in power.

### Formation of the Indira Congress

On **2 January 1978**, Indira Gandhi broke from the All India National Congress and formed the **Indira Congress**. Of 21 Congress Working Committee members, Kamalapati Tripathi, Syed Mir Qasim, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Ravindra Varma, Buta Singh, A.P. Sharma, and Maragatham Chandrasekhar stayed with her.

The AICC expelled Indira Gandhi from Congress on **8 January**. An Indira Congress convention was held in Hyderabad on **18 January**, and **Dr. Chenna Reddy** was appointed president of its state unit.

### Assembly Elections — Unexpected Results

In **February 1978**, elections were held for the Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka Assemblies. The results surprised political observers, as no party won a majority in the state.

| Party | Seats |
|---|---|
| Indira Congress | 175 |
| Janata | 60 |
| Congress ("Ruling Congress") | 30 |
| CPI + CPM | 8 |
| Independents | 15 |

Following this, **Vengala Rao's ministry resigned on 28 February 1978**.

concepts.partName: Five Chief Ministers in Five Years
concepts.bodyMd:
### 1\. Dr. M. Chenna Reddy

Since Indira Congress lacked a full majority, its state unit president and legislature-party leader, **Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy, took the oath as Chief Minister on 6 March 1978**. In that cabinet, **19 people became ministers for the first time**, with posts split between Andhra and Telangana at a **3:2 ratio**.

*   **Divi Kondaiah Chowdary** was elected unopposed as Speaker.
*   **K. Prabhakar Reddy** became Deputy Speaker.
*   Opposition leader **Gouthu Latchanna** was given ministerial rank.
*   **M.A. Aziz** became PCC president.

In **April 1978**, when Chenna Reddy and Karnataka CM Devaraj Urs went to Delhi, they told the high command not to interfere in their states' affairs. They believed internal party differences should be settled through mutual discussion, not through complaints to Delhi.

Even though Indira Gandhi, as party president, still tried to direct state Chief Ministers as if she were Prime Minister, both understood such directives no longer held automatic force. So when meeting her in Delhi, they simply absorbed dissatisfied groups' complaints and told her they would handle the issues themselves.

Within three months of taking office, dissatisfaction with Chenna Reddy began, and his fund-raising ventures came under sharp criticism. Indira Gandhi's victory in the **1980 Lok Sabha elections** and her return to power emboldened dissatisfied groups within the state.

**15 ministers signed an accusation letter** alleging he was misusing the administration for personal financial gain. Clashes between Chief Minister loyalists and dissidents reached a flashpoint, making central intervention unavoidable, yet Chenna Reddy did not go to Delhi and appeared favourable towards Indira Gandhi.

Of Indira Congress's 255 MLAs, **167 signed**, and of 40 MLC members, **29 signed**, demanding his removal. He called this a "disgraceful" state of affairs, and both sides stood their ground stubbornly.

Indira Gandhi, though usually able to resolve political problems quickly, had to bide her time on this occasion — or deliberately delayed while inflicting mental anguish on Chenna Reddy for resisting high-command interference in state affairs. His loyalists believed that very resistance had encouraged dissidents to turn against him.

The Congress (I) high command never let Andhra Pradesh Chief Ministers retire with dignity:

*   Dr. Chenna Reddy was kept in suspense for three months.
*   Dissidents were encouraged to abuse and oppose him.
*   Ministers refused to attend cabinet meetings.
*   Permission for an Assembly session or Panchayati Raj elections was withheld.

He was finally asked to send his resignation to the Governor. **Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy resigned as Chief Minister on 10 October 1980**, ending a three-month crisis after a tenure of **30 months**.

The party turmoil left Chenna Reddy medically affected after leaving office. Despite his reputation for courage, enterprise, able administration, and hard work, his lack of patience and restraint meant he could not retain everyone's affection — even his cabinet colleagues did not have much regard for him.

Corruption allegations during his tenure grew louder, and his failure to carefully disprove them damaged his government's public image. What mattered was not what he actually did but people's perception of it, a lesson that emerges from the political history of the last two decades.

As Chief Minister, he acted independently, conducting himself as a leader with his own internal-party discipline. He never treated the high command as sacrosanct, never gave up his individuality, and conducted himself as befitted the Chief Minister of a six-crore-person state who valued regional self-respect — he never governed despotically, regardless of who opposed him.

His downfall was not the work of dissidents alone: Indira Gandhi, feeling he had not shown her the loyalty she expected, removed him from his post.

### 2\. "Garibon Ka" Symbol — T. Anjaiah

Former Union minister **Tanguturi Anjaiah**, who had once worked as a daily-wage worker in the Alwyn Factory, took the oath as the state's eighth Chief Minister on **13 August 1980**, replacing Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy. Despite being seen as an ordinary, humble man, he became Chief Minister, trusted for his undisputed reputation, friendliness, and ability to unite everyone.

The Anjaiah ministry began with **22 members**. On **2 November 1980**, nine more were added, raising the total to **61** — the largest ministry in Andhra Pradesh's history.

Some who became ministers were not even Assembly members, and one who became a corporation chairman had not even won an election. All ministerial perks — official cars, bungalows, personal assistants — were made available to them. Of the Assembly's 291 total members, about a hundred received posts.

Anjaiah believed a large ministry made administration more effective, comparing it to an "Air Bus": the bigger the plane, the more comfortable the journey. He alone experienced full freedom in forming his ministry, and many were shocked at its size, though Indira Gandhi tolerated it out of personal regard at first.

As criticism mounted, she told him to reduce it, and within about ten weeks it was cut to **45**. Eleven months later, the same Anjaiah conducted the Panchayati Raj body elections.

Anjaiah's strength lay in Indira Gandhi's backing, so there was no rebellion against him within the party — he used to say he was ready to step down whenever the high command felt he should. Even though he took some democratic decisions and implemented them, he too could not remain in power long.

Undisciplined activities by ministers N. Janardhan Reddy and Kona Prabhakara Rao tarnished his ministry. N. Janardhan Reddy's political manoeuvring in Delhi enraged Rajiv Gandhi, who had Anjaiah publicly insulted and removed from his post.

During his tenure, government employees coordinated a unified stand. Anjaiah proved that a disciplined, law-abiding common man could rise to any heights, and he was also a strong encourager of the state's industrial sector.

### 3\. Bhavanam Venkatram

**Bhavanam Venkatram Reddy**, a member of the Legislative Council, took the oath as Chief Minister on **16 February 1982**, after Anjaiah. **C. Jagannatha Rao** of Telangana became Deputy Chief Minister.

Film actor **N.T. Rama Rao (NTR)** was by then preparing to launch a party, and since Bhavanam had no ability to counter him, the high command decided a more suitable person should be Chief Minister and asked Bhavanam to resign. He did so on **20 September 1982**, after a tenure of **6 months and 26 days**.

### 4\. Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy (first term)

The high command selected **Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy** after Bhavanam's resignation; he took the oath as Chief Minister on **20 September 1982**. The NTR wave had already begun sweeping the state by then, and believing only Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy could confront NTR, Delhi assured he would continue even after the upcoming elections.

Dr. Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy and Chandrababu Naidu served as ministers in his cabinet, while **G. Venkataswamy** became PCC president in this same period.

Congress Chief Ministers not completing full terms did not reflect a lack of ability — most had competence and administrative skill. But because Congress was a national party, they had to bow to high-command directives, which prevented them from fully demonstrating their strength and brought them disrepute. This proved a boon to the Telugu Desam Party.

The Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy government lasted **3 months and 19 days**. With Congress's defeat in the elections on **8 January 1983**, he resigned, and the Telugu Desam Party era began.

concepts.partName: The Emergence of the Telugu Desam Party
concepts.bodyMd:
### NTR's First Term

**Nandamuri Taraka Rama Rao** announced his entry into politics on **2 March 1982**, founded the **Telugu Desam Party** on **29 March**, and became its first president. In just four years, the state had seen four Chief Ministers change, anti-Congress sentiment had grown, and people wanted change.

The TDP received tremendous support in the **1983 elections**. It is rare worldwide for someone unfamiliar with politics to seize power within a few months, yet even locally unfamiliar candidates fielded by the TDP won on the strength of Rama Rao's personal appeal.

| Party | Seats |
|---|---|
| Telugu Desam | 202 |
| Congress | 60 |
| CPI | 4 |
| CPM | 5 |
| Janata | 1 |
| BJP | 3 |
| Majlis | 5 |
| Independents/others | 13 |

The NTR government took oath on **9 January 1983**. The first Mahanadu (party plenary) in Vijayawada in **May 1983** was a landmark in Indian political history, where leaders of 23 opposition parties — Left, centrist national parties, the BJP, and regional parties — discussed forming a unified opposition alliance.

From that day, NTR gained recognition as a statesman, though excessive workload began affecting his health. He went to America on **24 July 1984** for bypass surgery, which succeeded in Houston. From this point, dissatisfaction and rebellion began within the Telugu Desam Party.

While Rama Rao was in America, **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao**, calling himself "co-pilot" without either man's knowledge, began campaigning against him. Many signed a memorandum publicly declaring distrust in NTR and stating he no longer had a legislative majority.

Rama Rao returned to Hyderabad promptly on **14 August** and wrote to the Governor without delay, asking for Bhaskara Rao's removal. The Governor announced Bhaskara Rao's dismissal on the Chief Minister's advice.

Ministers T. Jeevan Reddy, Sanga Reddy, Satyanarayana, and Rama Muni Reddy resigned, creating turmoil within the party — citing 17 months of humiliation under the Chief Minister's autocratic style and resentment at being told they served only one party as a "private company." Bhaskara Rao told the Governor he had a majority, and Governor Ramlal believed him and swore him in as Chief Minister.

### Assessing the Removal of NTR

A grave mistake occurred with NTR's removal: it was neither the right time nor the right method. Rama Rao had, within his own party and among his own MLAs, been steadily losing respect, as corrupt practices, self-serving activities, alienating actions, and cancelled programmes eroded illusions about him.

A nationwide anti-Congress wave was building while Indira Gandhi's prestige was rising, so Rama Rao's isolation stemmed largely from his own conduct. Yet the political attack on him brought vast, undeserved sympathy, briefly making him a political hero.

Of 294 Assembly members, NTR had the support of **168**. Despite this majority, Governor Ramlal told him he had lost his majority and should resign. NTR was ready to bring his supporters to Raj Bhavan to prove his numbers, but the Governor refused to let him in — behaviour that drew widespread condemnation.

The Governor never tested the numbers of either Rama Rao's or Bhaskara Rao's supporters and refused to allow three days for verification, even though Rama Rao himself proved beyond doubt that he had a majority. The opposition used the opportunity to serve its own political interest.

Since the Telugu Desam Party had no comparable strength outside NTR, it had to depend on friendly parties in the crisis. All opposition parties, with the BJP and Communists playing a small role, sided with NTR. Rama Rao said Congress had funded the opposition to profit by using the organisation for its own gain.

Seeing nationwide agitation in NTR's favour, Indira Gandhi backed down. Governor Ramlal was recalled and **Shankar Dayal Sharma** appointed in his place. Nadendla could not prove his majority.

**NTR was reinstated on 16 September 1984**. The Assembly was dissolved on **27 September**, having lasted 22 months and 15 days from formation — even with an Assembly majority, the ministry felt a fresh public mandate was needed to restore political stability.

### The 30-Day Chief Minister

The Governor ordered the new Nadendla Bhaskara Rao government to prove its majority within 30 days — this could not be achieved. Fearing Governor dismissal, the **Nadendla ministry resigned on 16 September**, and the suspended Telugu Desam Party, through the same political manoeuvring, continued in power for another six months.

### NTR's Second Term

In mid-term elections held in **January 1985**, the Telugu Desam Party won a majority of over two-thirds, and NTR again became Chief Minister. His early goal was breaking Communist dominance, then Congress's strength — a goal not wrong in itself.

But the use of anti-social elements by political parties to achieve it had begun long before, and Vijayawada saw riots break out in this period, with murders occurring one after another, hidden behind unresolved crimes and dirty politics.

NTR was again elected party president in **1986**. By rule, he alone had authority to appoint the general secretary, and he wanted **Chandrababu Naidu** for the role; though some party members suggested the post go elsewhere, Chandrababu Naidu received it.

**P. Upendra** became the Telugu Desam Parliamentary Party president in Delhi. Around this time, Defence Minister V.P. Singh split from Rajiv Gandhi and founded "Jan Morcha."

Following NTR's lead on the Bofors issue, opposition MPs resigned their Parliament memberships on **24 July 1989**, four months before the Lok Sabha elections.

### The Rise and Fall of Upendra

No political party exists without satisfaction or dissatisfaction, and the Telugu Desam Party was no exception. As soon as Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's chapter closed, the general-secretary position fell to P. Upendra.

As the first chief secretary to serve as a loyal aide during TDP election campaigns, Upendra received honour within the party. He built connections between the TDP and national opposition parties, gaining significant benefits from those ties by drawing on his past acquaintance with veteran advisor-level leaders.

Many people whom Upendra had recommended, and to whom NTR gave Lok Sabha tickets, did not honour his recommendations for the Assembly elections. The seat Upendra sought was Tirupati; he was given Himayat Nagar instead, an area rife with Telangana and non-Telangana factional disputes — losing there was natural for him.

Suspecting he might rebel after losing, NTR confined Upendra's role to Delhi politics alone, sending him to the Rajya Sabha, where he carved out an important national position through his own skill. As his influence grew, NTR's affection for him grew too.

But in a party functioning on one person's charisma, no one would speak out against that person's authoritarianism, however smoothly things went. Even a daring dissenter would face NTR's wrath, as Upendra's later fall exemplifies. Chandrababu Naidu became general secretary in his place.

The **National Front** was formed with great fanfare on **6, 7, and 8 August 1988**, with NTR unanimously chosen as its president and V.P. Singh as convenor. Before the 1989 elections, opposition parties under the National Front reached a seat-sharing agreement.

The Front, allied with the Left and the BJP, together won about **300 seats**. **V.P. Singh became Prime Minister**, and TDP Rajya Sabha member P. Upendra received the Union Information and Broadcasting portfolio.

In the **1989 Assembly elections**:

| Party | Seats |
|---|---|
| Congress | 180 |
| TDP | 74 |
| CPI | 8 |
| CPM | 6 |
| BJP | 4 |
| Majlis | 4 |

Independents and other candidates won the remaining seats, and Congress returned to power in the state.

After the 1985 sweep, the TDP grew distant from influential classes. Government employees drifted away, trading communities became estranged over entry-tax issues, and backward classes who had placed hope in the TDP were left disappointed. Unemployment and rising education costs alienated the youth, and the party's foundations in the districts began to crumble.

"Family rule" became the excuse for many party pillars to crumble. The "Okkokkare" group — Nallapureddi Srinivasulu Reddy, Mudragada Padmanabham, K.E. Krishnamurthy, Janardhan Reddy, Vasantha Nageshwara Rao, Harirama Jogaiah, Penchalaiah, Ananda Gajapathi Raju, and Chintamohan — left the party. Their joining Congress benefited that side while the TDP lost out.

In a democracy, no party holds power permanently; changing fortunes by the people's wishes is a parliamentary tradition, and these elections made this undeniably clear.

### Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy (03-12-1989 to 07-12-1990)

Once Congress obtained a decisive majority, PCC president **Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy** became Chief Minister for the second time, taking oath in **December 1989**. This time, his rule began amid dissatisfaction, with two already-split camps making no effort to reconcile.

Rajasekhara Reddy's faction and Janardhan Reddy's faction were distinct dissatisfied groups within the cabinet. Rajasekhara Reddy's confrontation with Janardhan Reddy was relentless, like a street fight with no pause — Rajasekhara Reddy declared he was not accustomed to fighting halfway and retreating.

Even after returning from America, repeated trips to Delhi got Chenna Reddy no approval for reorganising his ministry, which only heightened dissatisfaction. Although the high command bore primary responsibility, only **Srinivasulu Reddy**, who had turned sharply against Chenna Reddy, escaped any loss of position — the Chief Minister lacked the will to treat him fairly even when he erred.

Setting up unprincipled backward-class welfare schemes and reducing them to a joke provoked further anger against himself, and his dealings, limited to a loyal coterie, naturally hurt many colleagues. The high command's own conduct — delaying corporation-chairman appointments and leadership decisions — contributed to his loss of prestige. Whenever he went to Delhi, however long he waited, he never got an interview with Rajiv Gandhi.

At the Centre, the V.P. Singh government collapsed after 11 months, failing to prove its majority on **7 November 1990**, and a Janata Dal (S) government formed under Chandrashekhar with Congress support.

Chief Minister Chenna Reddy failed severely in maintaining peace and order, especially in the capital. Communal riots in the first week of **December 1990** killed **71 people**, including 8 children — an unprecedented episode in Hyderabad's history.

Congress sent a five-member high-level delegation led by Balaram Jakhar to study conditions in the old city over three days. Rather than police or military handling the situation, the party delegation dealt directly with the Chief Minister, who had to follow its suggestions exactly.

The sudden communal riots, along with Minister Srinivasulu Reddy's resignation threats, created a severe crisis within the party — replacing Chenna Reddy would have severely hurt both the party's and Rajiv Gandhi's prestige.

During his tenure, Chenna Reddy scrapped many schemes introduced by the previous Telugu Desam government, dismantling and rebuilding systems NTR had scrapped. He was remembered for bringing World Bank loans to implement permanent schemes in cyclone-prone coastal districts.

His term ended amid celebrations, medical treatment, foreign travel, controversial statements and decisions, party dissatisfaction, refusal of high-command help, corruption scandals, Naxalite violence, and communal riots. Despite decades of political and administrative experience, his tenure ended this way. **Dr. Marri Chenna Reddy resigned as Chief Minister on 15 December 1990**.

### N. Janardhan Reddy (17-12-1990 to 9-10-1992)

**Nedurumalli Janardhan Reddy** became Chief Minister on **17 December 1990**, replacing Dr. Chenna Reddy. Since Dr. Bezawada Gopala Reddy became Chief Minister in 1955, leadership of the state had not returned to Nellore district until now, 35 years later.

Janardhan Reddy had remained tied to Congress throughout his career despite humiliations: he was denied a ticket and humiliated in the **1985 elections**, appointed state Congress president in **1988** and removed within three or four months in favour of Chenna Reddy. His long loyalty to the party and the Indira Gandhi family finally resulted in his becoming Chief Minister — a decade of waiting that yielded good results.

On taking charge, his decisions to abolish regional boards, give police freedom on the Naxalite issue, and continue the mandal system pleased Congress party members. A change in the government office and school working-hours system also pleased people generally, and teachers and government employees did not oppose it.

Differences between PCC president V. Hanumantha Rao and the Chief Minister surfaced openly during candidate selection for the **1991 Lok Sabha elections**. Some Congress workers pushed the Chief Minister to appoint their preferred names to government posts, and Hanumantha Rao could not get him to act on this.

He resolved to reduce his differences with the Chief Minister through his closeness to Rajiv Gandhi.

### Rajiv Gandhi's Assassination

On the night of **21 May 1991**, Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated near Sriperumbudur, close to Madras, while going to speak at an election meeting. His assassination, occurring mid-election, created problems threatening the party's very survival.

In the Lok Sabha elections held under these disturbed conditions, the Telugu Desam Party won the largest number of seats in the state, trying to reverse the 1989 result. But in constituencies voting after Rajiv Gandhi's death, it could not withstand the sympathy wave — neither NTR's campaign efforts nor his cinematic star power could overcome the sympathy vote.

### P.V. as Prime Minister

After Rajiv Gandhi's assassination, **P.V. Narasimha Rao** was made Congress party president, then became Prime Minister following the elections. He was not a member of Parliament when chosen, and needed election within a fortnight.

Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy had his own brother resign the Pulivendula seat so P.V. could contest and win it, avoiding any leverage Janardhan Reddy might otherwise gain by helping P.V. get elected. P.V., contesting a seat vacated for him, achieved a landslide victory.

The Chief Minister permitted 12 medical and 8 dental colleges in the state under the management quota, to collect capitation fees. The related Government Order, issued in **July 1992**, caused huge public outrage.

Student groups and political parties launched protests, and litigation proceeded in the High Court, which on **18 September 1992** struck down the G.O., observing that the permission had benefited relatives and associates of a "Janapriya" educational academy. Judges viewed this so severely that they denied the state government permission to appeal to the Supreme Court.

Even before this, dissatisfied groups' anger had been rising, and a high-command delegation from Delhi examined the state's political conditions and reported to the Prime Minister. No further action was needed, since time had rendered the High Court's decision moot.

Even though N. Janardhan Reddy had hoped to serve a full term, one signature on the medical-college files brought his tenure down within just **21 months**.

### Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy (second term)

**Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy** took the oath as Andhra Pradesh's fourteenth Chief Minister on **9 November 1992**, one of the most senior old-guard leaders aiming to build a new political edifice on moral, social, and economic reform. He earned women's affection across the state for banning arrack (liquor).

Unlike Chenna Reddy, he did not display autocratic tendencies, yet he could not earn a good reputation even among his own ministers and legislators. Corruption was less under his government than under Janardhan Reddy's, and his political standing, though lower than Chenna Reddy's or Janardhan Reddy's, did not make him disliked.

The people simply showed no particular enthusiasm towards him, since old-style politics no longer attracted them. Despite his political experience, blemish-free character, and good governance, he kept failing to strengthen the party for elections.

Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy appeared to do everything properly and systematically, but that alone did not guarantee good outcomes. Banning arrack deprived the state of revenue, and the token tax imposed to compensate caused severe public backlash.

Rising token and liquor prices pushed all commodity prices up disproportionately, burdening the common man — this caused visible public resentment against his government. His cabinet's large scale was not reduced either, and the discontent of those given generous ministerial posts across all sections was left largely unaddressed.

Kotla found it ironic that he had come to power a second time on NTR's help. His distinguishing trait was self-confidence to the point of stubbornness; he prioritised urgent matters and believed competent administration alone was his guiding philosophy, a trait he was praised for.

His own history and long administrative experience kept public dissatisfaction less visible despite unruly ministers, and his own colleagues lacked the courage to turn against him. PCC president Majji Tulasidas could not control the party's situation, and the Chief Minister made no attempt to fix it.

Frequent leadership changes led to frequent changes in development programmes, and by the time Kotla accepted the post, the party's state condition was already in severe decline. Yet in these two years he worked hard and enhanced the party's prestige. Had there been no internal party conflicts, and had dissatisfied factions shown discipline, these two years could have been remembered as golden years for the state.

As Assembly elections approached, various Congress factions prepared rival candidates against each other, dividing votes, and the party high command's efforts to resolve factional differences showed no result. The Chief Minister's stated view up to the elections was that infighting should be kept in check, but Dr. Rajasekhara Reddy's supporters carried out dissatisfaction activities blatantly, contributing most to the party's pitiable state.

Ruling party and opposition are two wheels of the democratic chariot; if one is excessive and the other too weak, development becomes impossible — a problem the state now faced. Congress won only **25 seats**, owing to visible internal factionalism, with its vote share falling below 35 percent.

The Telugu Desam Party's victory in **December 1994** proceeded like a triumphant march, in which many of Congress's "heavyweight" candidates lost together. Both Communist parties, TDP's allies, reaped seat-sharing rewards they had denied themselves for three decades. The TDP's victory exceeded even its own leaders' expectations.

_(Total: 292 seats.)_

Congress did not win a single seat in Adilabad, Karimnagar, Khammam, Mahbubnagar, Medak, Nalgonda, Rangareddy, Vizianagaram, and Visakhapatnam districts, winning only six seats across the whole of Telangana.

Before the elections, NTR fulfilled two promises: rice at two rupees a kilo, and total prohibition. Having clashed with the Congress government at the Centre before 1989, this time, as Chief Minister, he went to Delhi and asked P.V. Narasimha Rao to help build the Polavaram project and name it after him, trying to build cordial relations with, and secure assistance from, the Centre.

In **September 1993**, at a "Major Chandrakanth" centenary celebration in Tirupati, NTR announced on stage that he had married **Smt. Lakshmi Parvathi**, causing a great sensation — her entry into his life created a bigger stir than anything else.

After the TDP's landslide Assembly win, Lakshmi Parvathi, becoming a powerful figure, began playing her own role in the party. Those unwilling to accept her party control weakened within the party, and because of this **Chandrababu Naidu** took over the leadership.

NTR had to pay a heavy price for failing to recognise the importance of people's representatives in representative democracy. Party members who had campaigned tirelessly for months felt deeply hurt at being cast aside by him.

He continued to disregard, unhesitatingly, all opportunities available in politics, never giving MLAs their due respect — believing that if he snapped his fingers, they would come running wherever he was. Believing their own positions were at risk, MLAs coalesced around Chandrababu, forming a group and drawing closer to him.

Mixing up friendly words, unshakeable confidence that no one could confront him, and blind trust in his second wife together led to NTR's great political downfall.

Ordinarily, affection is weaker than power in politics. NTR's own popularity did not fade, but the power flowing to Chandrababu, though initially less, carried more institutional weight than the appeal flowing to NTR. Well-disciplined MLAs, legislators, and workers who had trusted NTR alone lost trust in him because of just one woman.

At the TDP's general body meeting on **30 August**, Chandrababu Naidu was unanimously elected party president, and after the resolution to remove NTR passed, Babu was announced as his replacement. **NTR resigned as Chief Minister on 30 August 1995.** With the slogan "I myself am the Telugu Desam — Telugu Desam is me," the man who ruled the party as sole leader for 13 years was swept away from power politics.

NTR's permanent place in the hearts of the state's people came not from politics but from cinema alone. He was an unmatched actor in the Telugu film industry, embodying virtues in every film — a widely known fact — and he portrayed villainy effortlessly on screen with ease.

He proved that same on-screen image could be changed into a clear-cut, straightforward Chief Minister, demonstrating this in 1983; but he was not an administrator, nor a political strategist. He won once. He lost once.

Aiming to become Chief Minister again, he promised rice at two rupees a kilo and declared prohibition to attract women — and won on these promises. These populist schemes cost the state up to **₹2,000 crore**, leaving the treasury empty.

### Friendship with the "Lotus" (BJP)

In the **1999 Assembly elections**, the Telugu Desam Party had to ally with the BJP. Of the state's eight Lok Sabha seats and 25 Assembly seats, TDP ceded its own share to the BJP.

Chandrababu Naidu had been supporting the Vajpayee government on outside-support terms since 1998, and the CPI and CPM, who had backed the TDP from the start, drifted away over this, leaving Chandrababu no path but to ally with the BJP.

The BJP itself was not keen on being given many constituencies — doing so risked letting it later use that base to become powerful in the state, aiming for power down the road. To prevent this, Chandrababu allotted the BJP only weaker constituencies.

Communist parties realised that standing alone risked being wiped out in the Lok Sabha elections. Believing an alliance might not even guarantee the votes needed for national-party recognition, the CPI/CPM fielded candidates in 90 Assembly and 12 Lok Sabha seats to boost their vote count, using TDP leader Harikrishna as a foil to defeat Chandrababu Naidu.

While the previous Assembly saw Congress win only 26 seats, in the new one it won **90 seats** — a confidence boost for that party. Nationally, the TDP emerged as the BJP's biggest ally with **29 seats**.

NTR's would-be successors, party leaders Lakshmi Parvathi and Nandamuri Harikrishna, failed to get their candidates elected, but their failure was not the reason Congress lost — Congress, despite all its efforts, failed to come close to power on its own.

No one had estimated the TDP would win with such a huge majority. Combined with goodwill for the Vajpayee government, Chandrababu's development programmes brought the TDP-BJP alliance **36 Lok Sabha seats** and **192 Assembly seats** — only slightly short of two-thirds in the Assembly. The Congress party was reduced to just **5 Lok Sabha seats**.

### Harikrishna

Legislator **Harikrishna**, who had joined Chandrababu against his own father in 1995, did not become a minister then, though he served as one for about six months later before growing estranged again, and did not get a ministry place when re-elected to the Assembly.

He began openly opposing party leader Chandrababu behind his back, and an indirect struggle developed between them. Harikrishna resigned his Assembly membership and founded the **"Anna Telugu Desam"** on **27 January 1999**.

### Change in Governance

Chandrababu Naidu's grand **1999** victory was important news not only for the state but for young India as a whole — he alone, at the time, dared to introduce populist schemes while also taking governance seriously.

The state had already fallen into significant debt by the time he took charge, since NTR's populist schemes as father-in-law and predecessor had left it in severe financial ruin, and anyone continuing those policies would have benefited politically from them.

Political leaders sheltering in such schemes — rice at two rupees a kilo, sarees at three rupees, free power, free housing, letting people roam Hyderabad's streets without work — saw themselves as fortunate deities granting people's wishes.

Chandrababu decided he had to overcome this situation, and even knowing this course would distance him from the people, he changed direction anyway.

He began telling people truthfully that appeasement schemes and outdated policies would not help, and that governance meant more than handouts, refusing to contribute to grand subsidy schemes like rice at two rupees a kilo. He made clear that good reasoning does not always guarantee political success, in the state or elsewhere.

In modernising government, he introduced computer methods, starting with land-record computerisation. A large share of court cases involved land disputes, and computerised records helped resolve them quickly and clearly, letting land ownership be checked with a mouse click from anywhere.

He launched Janmabhoomi programmes, and under the "Ryotu Bazaar" name, opened markets for farmers.

Having become one of the most influential figures in state politics after NTR, he had a personal vision to remain Chief Minister for another ten years. To achieve this, he introduced many schemes, going ahead of the World Bank to secure development funds, and undertook welfare schemes strictly within World Bank conditions rather than using irrigation and agriculture as tools of genuine economic empowerment.

He tried to please government officials with ad hoc daily allowances at short notice, implemented "people's rule" and Janmabhoomi-type schemes, arranged gas connections for women affected by firewood-stove smoke, and extended loans to DWCRA groups.

Despite all this, he lost the **2004 elections**. As soon as farmers felt left unattended, people began turning against him, and government employees, subjected to round-the-clock pressure of Janmabhoomi and constituent service without rest, grew increasingly alienated. As a result, he was defeated.

### Relations with the Centre

From 1995, Chandrababu Naidu began occupying a key role in national politics. In the "hung" Lok Sabha of **1996**, when the TDP had **16 Lok Sabha seats**, he played the leading role in shaping the United Front as an alternative to Congress and the BJP.

The BJP, as the largest party, formed a government under Vajpayee, which lasted only **13 days** before resigning for lack of majority. The United Front government then came to power with Congress support, with Chandrababu Naidu pulling the strings, and the Telugu Desam Party shared in that government's power.

In the **1998 elections**, again no party won a majority. TDP won **12 Lok Sabha seats** and played a pivotal role; Chandrababu Naidu played a leading national role in forming the NDA coalition with the BJP, and from then shone in national politics.

The TDP accepted the Lok Sabha Speaker's post but declared support from outside the government, and when ally DMK withdrew support, the NDA government fell within **13 months**.

In the **1999 elections**, the TDP again contested with the NDA and swept **29 Lok Sabha seats** in the state, again agreeing to support the government from outside and accepting only the Speaker's post. That post went to Balayogi, who could not continue owing to an accident-related death.

BJP leaders respected Chandrababu Naidu for behaving as a reliable ally, and whatever the state needed from the Centre, he obtained without delay. Despite the alliance's frictions with other parties, only the TDP created no problems for the BJP, giving Chandrababu more prominence than other leaders.

While United Front governments were in power, Chandrababu took his role as the front's chief strategist seriously, spending an inordinate amount of time flying between Delhi and the state at the Chief Minister's own cost to maintain his grip in Delhi. Ramakrishna Hegde, NTR, and Devi Lal had earlier carried the main responsibility of guiding national politics from the states; this role now passed to Chandrababu.

While in power, he elevated information technology to the neglect of other sectors. In truth, his rule brought more harm than good to the state's people — his policies suited countries with small populations, not a country with a large one, least of all his own state.

In healthcare, for example, thousands of jobs in developing government institutions were handed to VRS (voluntary retirement) and outsourced under World Bank terms, under the pretext of increasing efficiency, citing West Bengal CM Jyoti Basu's record as precedent.

Telugu people grew disillusioned with Chandrababu's ambitions. With overweening self-confidence, believing no one else had his political-strategy skill, he underestimated Congress's resurgence, trusting no fellow leader within the party and relying only on officials' statistics and reports.

Without recognising ground-level realities, he formed opinions about every matter in advance, never changed his position regardless of circumstances, and hence could not build a group of leaders loyal to him beyond himself — nor did he allow leaders with grassroots support within the party to rise above a certain level.

Using some populist scheme or other, even in unfavourable circumstances, became Chandrababu's habitual tactic; whether these schemes brought genuine benefit or reached the people, or merely served his publicity, was known to him alone. Whenever one scheme ended, he would announce a new one — this was his pattern, focused more on presenting a polished image and administrative reputation than on genuine implementation.

For example, one week after a successful public programme, in **October 1995**, he abruptly ended it and began the "Shramadaan" (voluntary labour) scheme, personally picking up a broom to sweep streets. Fearing his new schemes would lose their announcement-worthy shine, he would suddenly inspect government offices and hospitals, often without the officials responsible for those departments present.

He conducted several public-awareness tours, holding meetings at village, mandal, revenue-division, and town levels, explaining how far his government had resolved people's problems — and the public accepted these new schemes with sudden interest each time, following this same pattern.
